records.source: כִּי־יִמָּצֵ֣א חָלָ֗ל בָּאֲדָמָה֙ אֲשֶׁר֩ יְהוָ֨ה אֱלֹהֶ֜יךָ נֹתֵ֤ן לְךָ֙ לְרִשְׁתָּ֔הּ נֹפֵ֖ל בַּשָּׂדֶ֑ה לֹ֥א נוֹדַ֖ע מִ֥י הִכָּֽהוּ׃
records.gloss: If is found [one] slain in the land which Yahweh your God [is] giving to you to possess it, lying in the field, not is known who struck him,
pieces: If someone is found slain, lying in the open country in the land that {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} your God is giving you to take possession of, and no one knows who struck the victim down,

L.1: If one slain is found in the land that {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} your God is giving you to take possession of, lying in the field, [and] it is not known who struck him down,

R.1: The body of someone who was killed may be found lying in an open field in the land that {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} your God is giving you to take as your own. No one knows who killed that person.

decisions.choice: one slain: a person killed by violence
decisions.reason: The word describes someone pierced or struck down, a person who died by another's hand, not by accident or illness. The same word is used of those killed in battle (Numbers 19:16; 1 Samuel 31:1). Here the death is a killing, but the killer is unknown.

decisions.choice: a killing with no witness and no suspect
decisions.reason: The law usually needs witnesses to convict a killer (17:6; 19:15), and the cities of refuge deal with killers who are known (19:1-13). This case covers what those laws cannot: a murder no one can solve. Blood shed and left unanswered was thought to bring guilt on the land and its people (19:10; Numbers 35:33), so the community still has to act.

decisions.choice: the slain one, him: any victim, man or woman
decisions.reason: The word for the slain person and the pronoun that refers to it are masculine, the ordinary way the language speaks of a person in general. The law applies to any victim.

decisions.choice: if: the start of a case that runs to verse 9
decisions.reason: The word opens a case law. Verse 1 sets out the situation; verses 2-8 describe what the leaders and the nearest town must do, and verse 9 gives the result.

decisions.choice: the victim / that person
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say "the victim" and "that person" for "him", since the law covers anyone found killed. Literal keeps "him".

decisions.choice: open country / open field
decisions.reason: The word for "field" means land outside the towns, whether farmed or wild. Balanced says "open country" so that it is not taken to mean only a planted field.

records.heading: When someone is found slain

records.source: וְיָצְא֥וּ זְקֵנֶ֖יךָ וְשֹׁפְטֶ֑יךָ וּמָדְדוּ֙ אֶל־הֶ֣עָרִ֔ים אֲשֶׁ֖ר סְבִיבֹ֥ת הֶחָלָֽל׃
records.gloss: And will go out your elders and your judges and will measure to the cities which [are] around the slain [one].
pieces: your elders and your judges are to go out and measure the distance from the body to each of the towns around it.

L.2: then your elders and your judges shall go out and measure [the distance] to the cities that [are] around the slain [one].

R.2: Then your elders and judges must go out to that place. They must measure how far it is from the body to each of the towns nearby.

decisions.choice: your elders and your judges: leaders who act for the whole people
alternatives: the elders and judges of the towns around the body
decisions.reason: Elders were the senior men who led a town or the nation (19:12; 22:15); judges were appointed in every town to decide cases (16:18). The text speaks of "your" elders and judges, addressing Israel as a whole, and only in verse 3 brings in the elders of the nearest town. So these may be leaders from outside the area, who can settle fairly which town is nearest, though the text does not say who they are.

decisions.choice: measure to the cities: find which town is closest
decisions.reason: They measure from the place where the body lies to the surrounding towns. The point is to find the nearest town (verse 3), which then has to answer for the blood shed near it.

decisions.choice: the distance
decisions.reason: The Hebrew says only "measure to the cities". Literal adds "[the distance]" in brackets, and Balanced and Readable say it plainly, so that it is clear what is being measured.

records.source: וְהָיָ֣ה הָעִ֔יר הַקְּרֹבָ֖ה אֶל־הֶחָלָ֑ל וְלָֽקְח֡וּ זִקְנֵי֩ הָעִ֨יר הַהִ֜וא עֶגְלַ֣ת בָּקָ֗ר אֲשֶׁ֤ר לֹֽא־עֻבַּד֙ בָּ֔הּ אֲשֶׁ֥ר לֹא־מָשְׁכָ֖ה בְּעֹֽל׃
records.gloss: And will be the city the nearest to the slain [one], and will take [the] elders of the city the that a heifer of [the] herd which not has been worked with her, which not has pulled in a yoke.
pieces: The elders of the town nearest the body are to take a heifer from the herd that has never been put to work and has never pulled in a yoke.

L.3: And the city that is nearest to the slain [one]: the elders of that city shall take a heifer of the herd that has not been worked with [and] that has not pulled in a yoke.

R.3: The elders of the town closest to the body must choose a young cow that has never been made to work or worn a yoke.

decisions.choice: the nearest city is named first: the duty falls on it
decisions.reason: The sentence starts with the town nearest the body, then names its elders. The order makes the point of the measuring: that town, and no other, must carry out the ritual and clear itself.

decisions.choice: a heifer never worked or yoked: an animal untouched by ordinary use
decisions.reason: A heifer is a young cow that has not yet borne a calf. This one must never have worked in the fields or pulled under a yoke. Animals set aside for a sacred act were often required to be unused in this way, as with the red heifer (Numbers 19:2) and the cows that drew the ark (1 Samuel 6:7).

decisions.choice: young cow
decisions.reason: Readable says "young cow" for "heifer", a word many young readers do not know. Literal and Balanced keep "heifer".

decisions.choice: And the city that is nearest to the slain [one]:
decisions.reason: Literal keeps the Hebrew order, which names the town first and then starts again with its elders; the colon shows the break. Balanced and Readable make one ordinary sentence.

records.source: וְהוֹרִ֡דוּ זִקְנֵי֩ הָעִ֨יר הַהִ֤וא אֶת־הָֽעֶגְלָה֙ אֶל־נַ֣חַל אֵיתָ֔ן אֲשֶׁ֛ר לֹא־יֵעָבֵ֥ד בּ֖וֹ וְלֹ֣א יִזָּרֵ֑עַ וְעָֽרְפוּ־שָׁ֥ם אֶת־הָעֶגְלָ֖ה בַּנָּֽחַל׃
records.gloss: And will bring down [the] elders of the city the that the heifer to a wadi ever-flowing which not is worked in it and not is sown, and they will break the neck there [of] the heifer in the wadi.
pieces: The elders of that town are to lead the heifer down to a valley with a stream that never runs dry, on land that is neither plowed nor sown, and there in the valley they are to break the heifer's neck.

L.4: And the elders of that city shall bring the heifer down to a valley with an ever-flowing stream, which is not worked and not sown, and they shall break the heifer's neck there in the valley.

R.4: They must lead the cow down to a valley where a stream always flows. It must be land that is not plowed or planted. There in the valley they must break the cow's neck.

decisions.choice: a valley with an ever-flowing stream
decisions.reason: The word for the valley names a stream bed that is often dry outside the rainy season. The word with it means "lasting, enduring", and is used of a stream that never fails (Amos 5:24; Psalm 74:15). Here it most likely names a valley whose water always runs. It could also mean a valley that is "permanent" in the sense of rough and rocky, never broken up by farming, which would fit the rest of the verse.

decisions.choice: not worked and not sown: uncultivated ground
decisions.reason: The two verbs describe land that is not farmed. The form can mean land that has never been farmed, or land that from now on is not to be farmed; either way, the ritual takes place away from the fields that feed the people.

decisions.choice: break the heifer's neck: a killing that is not an altar sacrifice
decisions.reason: The heifer is not slaughtered at an altar, and no blood is caught or sprinkled. Breaking the neck is the way an unredeemed firstborn donkey was put to death (Exodus 13:13; 34:20). The text does not explain the rite. It seems to stand for the death the unknown killer deserves, carried out away from the farmland, so that the guilt of the blood is dealt with.

decisions.choice: valley
decisions.reason: The Hebrew word names a stream bed in a narrow valley. All three levels say "valley" and, where the stream is meant, say so; the technical word "wadi" would be strange to most readers.

records.source: וְנִגְּשׁ֣וּ הַכֹּהֲנִים֮ בְּנֵ֣י לֵוִי֒ כִּ֣י בָ֗ם בָּחַ֞ר יְהוָ֤ה אֱלֹהֶ֨יךָ֙ לְשָׁ֣רְת֔וֹ וּלְבָרֵ֖ךְ בְּשֵׁ֣ם יְהוָ֑ה וְעַל־פִּיהֶ֥ם יִהְיֶ֖ה כָּל־רִ֥יב וְכָל־נָֽגַע׃
records.gloss: And will come near the priests, [the] sons of Levi, for them has chosen Yahweh your God to minister to him and to bless in [the] name of Yahweh, and on their mouth will be every dispute and every wound.
pieces: The priests, the sons of Levi, are to step forward. {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} your God has chosen them to serve {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} and to pronounce blessings in the name of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, and their word is to settle every dispute and every case of assault.

L.5: And the priests, the sons of Levi, shall come near, for {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} your God has chosen them to serve {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} and to bless in the name of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, and by their mouth every dispute and every assault shall be [settled].

R.5: The priests from the tribe of Levi must come there too. {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} your God has chosen them to serve {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} and to bless the people in the name of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}. They are the ones who decide every dispute and every case where someone has been hurt.

decisions.choice: the priests, the sons of Levi: the priests from Levi's tribe
decisions.reason: This is the usual way Deuteronomy names the priests (17:9, 18; 18:1; 31:9). It stresses that the priesthood belongs to the tribe the LORD set apart (10:8).

decisions.choice: the reason for the priests' presence: their word settles cases
decisions.reason: The priests are given no words or actions in the rite. The verse says why they are there: they serve the LORD, bless in his name, and give the final decision in hard cases (17:8-9). Their presence puts the whole act under the LORD's authority.

decisions.choice: every dispute and every assault
decisions.reason: The second word means a blow or a stroke; it is also used for a mark of skin disease (24:8). Beside "dispute" it means a case of injury or violence, as in the list of hard cases in 17:8.

decisions.choice: on their mouth: by their word
decisions.reason: The "mouth" here is what the priests say: their ruling decides the matter (compare 17:10-11).

decisions.choice: [settled] / settled; to bless the people
decisions.reason: The Hebrew says only that every dispute "shall be on their mouth". Literal adds "[settled]" in brackets and Balanced says it plainly. Readable adds "the people" as the ones the priests bless (Numbers 6:23-27).

records.source: וְכֹ֗ל זִקְנֵי֙ הָעִ֣יר הַהִ֔וא הַקְּרֹבִ֖ים אֶל־הֶחָלָ֑ל יִרְחֲצוּ֙ אֶת־יְדֵיהֶ֔ם עַל־הָעֶגְלָ֖ה הָעֲרוּפָ֥ה בַנָּֽחַל׃
records.gloss: And all [the] elders of the city the that, the near to the slain [one], shall wash their hands over the heifer the broken-necked in the wadi.
pieces: Then all the elders of the town nearest the body are to wash their hands in the valley over the heifer whose neck was broken.

L.6: And all the elders of that city, who are nearest to the slain [one], shall wash their hands over the heifer whose neck was broken in the valley.

R.6: Then all the elders of the town nearest the body must wash their hands over the dead cow in the valley.

decisions.choice: washing the hands: a sign of innocence
decisions.reason: Washing the hands showed that a person had no part in a killing (Psalm 26:6; 73:13). The elders act out what they then say in verse 7. Done over the dead heifer, it ties their statement to the rite.

decisions.choice: the near ones: the elders as the town's representatives
decisions.reason: The word "nearest" is plural and goes with the elders: they speak for the town that lies closest to the body.

decisions.choice: the dead cow
decisions.reason: Readable says "the dead cow" for "the heifer whose neck was broken", since verse 4 has just described how it died.

records.source: וְעָנ֖וּ וְאָמְר֑וּ יָדֵ֗ינוּ לֹ֤א שָֽׁפְכוּ֙ אֶת־הַדָּ֣ם הַזֶּ֔ה וְעֵינֵ֖ינוּ לֹ֥א רָאֽוּ׃
records.gloss: And they shall answer and say, our hands not shed the blood the this, and our eyes not saw.
pieces: They are to declare, 'Our hands did not shed this blood, and our eyes did not see it done.

L.7: And they shall answer and say, 'Our hands did not shed this blood, and our eyes did not see [it].

R.7: They must say, 'We did not kill this person, and we did not see who did it.

decisions.choice: did not shed (plural): the reading the Hebrew text marks to be read
decisions.reason: The consonants written in the Hebrew text spell a singular verb, "has not shed", with "our hands" taken together. The scribes' note in the margin says to read the plural, "did not shed", which agrees with "our hands". The pinned data follows the marked reading. The meaning is the same either way.

decisions.choice: answer and say: make a formal declaration
decisions.reason: "Answer" here does not mean replying to a question. The verb is used for a solemn statement before witnesses, as in 26:5 and 27:15. The elders speak for their town in a public, legal way.

decisions.choice: our hands did not shed this blood, our eyes did not see: we are not guilty and know nothing
decisions.reason: To "shed blood" is to kill (19:10). The elders declare that no one of their town did it and that they did not witness it, so they cannot name the killer. Their declaration continues as a prayer in verse 8.

decisions.choice: We did not kill this person, and we did not see who did it.
decisions.reason: Readable says plainly what the two pictures of the hands and eyes mean.

records.source: כַּפֵּר֩ לְעַמְּךָ֨יִשְׂרָאֵ֤ל אֲשֶׁר־פָּדִ֨יתָ֙ יְהוָ֔ה וְאַל־תִּתֵּן֙ דָּ֣ם נָקִ֔י בְּקֶ֖רֶב עַמְּךָ֣ יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל וְנִכַּפֵּ֥ר לָהֶ֖ם הַדָּֽם׃
records.gloss: Make atonement for your people Israel whom you redeemed, Yahweh, and not put blood innocent in [the] midst of your people Israel. And will be atoned for them the blood.
pieces: Make atonement for {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} people Israel, whom {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} redeemed, {{divine_name:LORD|Yahweh}}, and do not hold the guilt of innocent blood against {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} people Israel.' Then the bloodshed will be atoned for on their behalf.

L.8: Make atonement for {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} people Israel, whom {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} redeemed, O {{divine_name:LORD|Yahweh}}, and do not put innocent blood in the midst of {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} people Israel.' And the blood shall be atoned for them.

R.8: {{divine_name:LORD|Yahweh}}, make atonement for {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} people Israel, whom {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} set free. Do not blame {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} people for the death of an innocent person.' Then the guilt for that death will be taken away from them.

decisions.choice: the prayer continues the elders' declaration
decisions.reason: No new speaker is named, so the prayer goes on from the elders' words in verse 7. Some take it as spoken by the priests of verse 5, but the text gives them no words. The last sentence of the verse, in the third person, is not part of the prayer: it is Moses' promise of the result.

decisions.choice: make atonement: cover and remove guilt
decisions.reason: The verb means to cover over or wipe away guilt so that it no longer stands against someone. With the LORD as the one asked to act, it amounts to pardoning the people. No sacrifice is offered on an altar; the rite and the prayer together ask God to take the guilt away. The second verb has an unusual form, but its sense is passive: the blood "will be atoned for".

decisions.choice: redeemed: set free, as from slavery
decisions.reason: The verb means to ransom, to free someone by paying or acting for them. Deuteronomy uses it for the LORD's rescue of Israel from Egypt (7:8; 9:26; 13:6). The elders appeal to what the LORD has already done for his people.

decisions.choice: do not put innocent blood in the midst of your people: do not hold them guilty of the killing
decisions.reason: "Innocent blood" is the blood of someone killed who did not deserve to die. To "put" it among the people is to count its guilt against them (19:10; Jonah 1:14). The prayer asks that the guilt of the unsolved murder not rest on Israel.

decisions.choice: hold the guilt of innocent blood against / blame ... for the death of an innocent person
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say what "put innocent blood" means. Readable says "set free" for "redeemed" and puts the vocative first, as English often does in prayer.

records.source: וְאַתָּ֗ה תְּבַעֵ֛ר הַדָּ֥ם הַנָּקִ֖י מִקִּרְבֶּ֑ךָ כִּֽי־תַעֲשֶׂ֥ה הַיָּשָׁ֖ר בְּעֵינֵ֥י יְהוָֽה׃ס
records.gloss: And you, you shall purge the blood the innocent from your midst, for you shall do the right in [the] eyes of Yahweh.
pieces: In this way you will purge the guilt of innocent blood from among you, for you will be doing what is right in the sight of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}.

L.9: And you shall purge the innocent blood from your midst, for you shall do what [is] right in the eyes of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}.

R.9: This is how you will remove the guilt of killing an innocent person from among you. You will be doing what {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} says is right.

decisions.choice: and you: the whole people, made responsible
decisions.reason: The Hebrew adds the pronoun "you" for emphasis. The killer is unknown, but Israel itself must deal with the guilt, and it does so by carrying out this law.

decisions.choice: purge the innocent blood from your midst: remove the guilt of the killing from the community
decisions.reason: The verb means to burn away and so to clear out completely, as in the phrase "purge the evil from your midst" (13:6; 19:13). Here it is the guilt of innocent blood that is removed.

decisions.choice: right in the eyes of the LORD: what the LORD judges to be right
decisions.reason: The phrase sets the LORD's judgment as the standard (6:18; 12:25, 28; 13:19).

decisions.choice: the guilt of
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable add "the guilt of", since what is removed is not the blood itself but the guilt it brings. Literal keeps "the innocent blood".

records.source: כִּֽי־תֵצֵ֥א לַמִּלְחָמָ֖ה עַל־אֹיְבֶ֑יךָ וּנְתָנ֞וֹ יְהוָ֧ה אֱלֹהֶ֛יךָ בְּיָדֶ֖ךָ וְשָׁבִ֥יתָ שִׁבְיֽוֹ׃
records.gloss: When you go out to war against your enemies, and gives him Yahweh your God into your hand, and you take captive his captives,
pieces: When you go out to war against your enemies and {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} your God hands them over to you and you take some of them captive,

L.10: When you go out to war against your enemies, and {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} your God gives them into your hand, and you take captives from them,

R.10: You may go to war against your enemies, and {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} your God may give you victory over them. You may take some of them as prisoners.

decisions.choice: him, his captives: the enemy spoken of as one
decisions.reason: After the plural "enemies", the Hebrew says "gives him" and "his captives", treating the enemy as a single body. The sense is plural: the enemies and the people taken from them.

decisions.choice: give into your hand: put in your power, give victory
decisions.reason: The phrase means that the LORD lets Israel defeat the enemy (2:24; 7:24; 20:13). The victory is his gift.

decisions.choice: a war against distant enemies
decisions.reason: The rules for war in chapter 20 allow women and children to be taken captive from cities far away (20:14-15), but not from the peoples of the land, who were to be devoted to destruction (20:16-18). This law, which runs to verse 14, belongs to the first kind of war.

decisions.choice: them
decisions.reason: All three levels say "them" for the Hebrew "him" and "his", since "enemies" has just been named in the plural. Literal would otherwise seem to speak of one person or even of God.

decisions.choice: give you victory over them; as prisoners
decisions.reason: Readable says what "give into your hand" means, and says "prisoners" for "captives".

records.heading: Women taken captive

records.source: וְרָאִיתָ֙ בַּשִּׁבְיָ֔ה אֵ֖שֶׁת יְפַת־תֹּ֑אַר וְחָשַׁקְתָּ֣ בָ֔הּ וְלָקַחְתָּ֥ לְךָ֖ לְאִשָּֽׁה׃
records.gloss: and you see among the captives a woman beautiful of form, and you desire her, and you take [her] for yourself as a wife,
pieces: and you see among the captives a beautiful woman whom you desire and want to marry,

L.11: and you see among the captives a woman beautiful in form, and you desire her and take [her] for yourself as a wife,

R.11: Among them you may see a beautiful woman. You may be attracted to her and want to marry her.

decisions.choice: desire her: set your heart on her
decisions.reason: The verb means to be strongly drawn to someone or something, to set one's love on it. Deuteronomy uses it of the LORD's love for Israel's ancestors (7:7; 10:15). Here it is a man's desire for a woman.

decisions.choice: take her as a wife: the man means to marry her
decisions.reason: This clause still belongs to the condition that began in verse 10; what the man must do comes in verses 12-14. The law allows him to have the woman only as a wife, and only after the waiting set out in verse 13.

decisions.choice: you: each Israelite man
decisions.reason: The "you" here is singular and masculine: the law addresses the individual soldier who wants to marry a captive.

decisions.choice: want to marry
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say "want to marry her" for "take her as a wife", because the marriage itself does not happen until verse 13. Literal keeps the Hebrew wording.

records.source: וַהֲבֵאתָ֖הּ אֶל־תּ֣וֹךְ בֵּיתֶ֑ךָ וְגִלְּחָה֙ אֶת־רֹאשָׁ֔הּ וְעָשְׂתָ֖ה אֶת־צִפָּרְנֶֽיהָ׃
records.gloss: and you shall bring her into [the] midst of your house, and she shall shave her head and do her nails,
pieces: you are to bring her into your home. She is to shave her head, trim her nails,

L.12: then you shall bring her into the midst of your house, and she shall shave her head and do her nails,

R.12: Bring her into your home. She must shave her head and cut her nails.

decisions.choice: shaving the head and doing the nails: signs of leaving her old life
decisions.reason: The text does not explain these acts. Shaving the head marked mourning in many nations around Israel (Isaiah 15:2; Jeremiah 41:5) and the end of a time of separation (Leviticus 14:8-9; Numbers 6:9). Here, with the change of clothes in verse 13, they mark that the woman's former life has ended and a new one is beginning in Israel.

decisions.choice: do her nails: most likely trim them
decisions.reason: The verb is simply "do" or "make". It is used of caring for the beard in 2 Samuel 19:25, so here it most likely means trimming the nails, a sign of a fresh start. It could instead mean letting them grow, as a sign of mourning, like neglecting the beard.

decisions.choice: then: what the man must do begins here
decisions.reason: After the condition in verses 10-11, this verse begins the rules the man must follow. The sentence runs on into verse 13.

decisions.choice: trim / cut
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable give the likely sense of "do" (m2). Literal keeps the plain verb, which leaves the question open.

records.source: וְהֵסִ֩ירָה֩ אֶת־שִׂמְלַ֨ת שִׁבְיָ֜הּ מֵעָלֶ֗יהָ וְיָֽשְׁבָה֙ בְּבֵיתֶ֔ךָ וּבָֽכְתָ֛ה אֶת־אָבִ֥יהָ וְאֶת־אִמָּ֖הּ יֶ֣רַח יָמִ֑ים וְאַ֨חַר כֵּ֜ן תָּב֤וֹא אֵלֶ֨יהָ֙ וּבְעַלְתָּ֔הּ וְהָיְתָ֥ה לְךָ֖ לְאִשָּֽׁה׃
records.gloss: and she shall remove [the] clothing of her captivity from on her, and she shall stay in your house and weep for her father and her mother a month of days; and after so you shall go in to her and be her husband, and she shall be to you as a wife.
pieces: and take off the clothes she was wearing when she was captured. She is to stay in your house and mourn for her father and mother a full month. After that you may sleep with her and be her husband, and she will be your wife.

L.13: and she shall remove the clothing of her captivity from herself, and she shall stay in your house and weep for her father and her mother a month of days; and after that you may go in to her and be her husband, and she shall be your wife.

R.13: She must take off the clothes she wore when she was captured. She will live in your house and mourn for her father and mother for a whole month. After that you may sleep with her and become her husband, and she will be your wife.

decisions.choice: the clothing of her captivity: what she wore when she was taken
decisions.reason: These are the clothes in which she was captured, her dress as a woman of another nation. Taking them off goes with the shaving of verse 12: she puts off her old place and status.

decisions.choice: weep for her father and mother a full month: a time of mourning
decisions.reason: Her parents may have died in the war, and in any case she has lost them and her home. Thirty days was a full time of mourning, as for Aaron and for Moses (Numbers 20:29; Deuteronomy 34:8). The law gives her this time before the marriage.

decisions.choice: go in to her and be her husband: begin the marriage
decisions.reason: To "go in to" a woman is the common way of speaking of sexual union (22:13). The second verb means to become a husband, to take a wife. The waiting comes first; only then may the marriage begin, and she becomes his wife, not his slave (verse 14).

decisions.choice: sleep with her
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say "sleep with her" for "go in to her", the plain English way of naming sexual union. Literal keeps the Hebrew expression.

decisions.choice: a full month / a whole month
decisions.reason: "A month of days" means a complete month. Balanced and Readable say so; Literal keeps the Hebrew phrase.

records.source: וְהָיָ֞ה אִם־לֹ֧א חָפַ֣צְתָּ בָּ֗הּ וְשִׁלַּחְתָּהּ֙ לְנַפְשָׁ֔הּ וּמָכֹ֥ר לֹא־תִמְכְּרֶ֖נָּה בַּכָּ֑סֶף לֹא־תִתְעַמֵּ֣ר בָּ֔הּ תַּ֖חַת אֲשֶׁ֥ר עִנִּיתָֽהּ׃ס
records.gloss: And it will be, if not you delight in her, and you shall let her go as she wishes, and sell surely not you shall sell her for money; not you shall treat as a slave her, because that you have humbled her.
pieces: But if you are no longer pleased with her, you are to let her go free wherever she wishes. You must never sell her for money or treat her as a slave, because you have dishonored her.

L.14: And it shall be, if you do not delight in her, then you shall let her go as she wishes, but you shall certainly not sell her for money; you shall not treat her as a slave, because you have humbled her.

R.14: But you may later decide you do not want her. Then you must let her go free to live wherever she wants. You must never sell her or treat her as a slave, because you have brought shame on her.

decisions.choice: if you do not delight in her: if you no longer want her as your wife
decisions.reason: The man has married her (verse 13) and later turns against her. Letting her go is a divorce, like the one 24:1 describes.

decisions.choice: let her go as she wishes: she goes free, where she chooses
decisions.reason: The phrase means "according to her own desire". She is not returned to captivity or handed to someone else; she leaves as a free woman and may go where she wants.

decisions.choice: treat her as a slave: deal with her as property
decisions.reason: The verb is rare; it appears only here and in 24:7, where it is used of kidnapping and selling a person. It seems to mean treating someone as goods to be used or sold. Together with "sell her" it rules out any return to slavery.

decisions.choice: you have humbled her: you have dishonored her
decisions.reason: The verb means to bring someone low. Used of a woman, it means to take her sexually and so bring shame on her (22:24, 29; Genesis 34:2). He took her as his wife and then sent her away; because of that wrong, he loses any right over her.

decisions.choice: sell her; treat her as a slave
decisions.reason: This sentence is about selling a person as property, so every level keeps the word "slave", as the style guide asks where people are bought and sold.

decisions.choice: let her go free
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable add "free" to bring out the point of "as she wishes": she leaves with her freedom.

records.source: כִּֽי־תִהְיֶ֨יןָ לְאִ֜ישׁ שְׁתֵּ֣י נָשִׁ֗ים הָאַחַ֤ת אֲהוּבָה֙ וְהָאַחַ֣ת שְׂנוּאָ֔ה וְיָֽלְדוּ־ל֣וֹ בָנִ֔ים הָאֲהוּבָ֖ה וְהַשְּׂנוּאָ֑ה וְהָיָ֛ה הַבֵּ֥ן הַבְּכ֖וֹר לַשְּׂנִיאָֽה׃
records.gloss: If they belong to a man two wives, the one loved and the one hated, and they bear to him sons, the loved and the hated, and is the son the firstborn to the hated,
pieces: If a man has two wives, one he loves and one he does not, and both have borne him sons, but the firstborn son is the son of the unloved wife,

L.15: If a man has two wives, the one loved and the other hated, and they have borne him sons, both the loved and the hated, and the firstborn son belongs to the hated one,

R.15: A man may have two wives. He may love one of them more than the other. Both may have sons by him, and the firstborn son may belong to the wife he loves less.

decisions.choice: loved and hated: loved more and loved less
decisions.reason: In family matters "hated" often means loved less, not hated in the full sense. Jacob loved Rachel "more than Leah", and Leah is then called "hated" (Genesis 29:30-31). The law is about a wife who is not favored.

decisions.choice: a man with two wives
decisions.reason: The law does not approve of having two wives; it deals with a family where this has happened and protects those who could be wronged. The story of Jacob's family shows the rivalry such a household could bring (Genesis 29-30).

decisions.choice: the firstborn son: the father's first son
decisions.reason: The firstborn is the first son born to the father, whichever wife is his mother (verse 17). He had a special place in the family and a larger share of the inheritance.

decisions.choice: unloved / loves less
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say "unloved" and "loves less" for "hated", which in English sounds far stronger than the Hebrew means here (m1). Literal keeps "hated".

records.heading: The right of the firstborn

records.source: וְהָיָ֗ה בְּיוֹם֙ הַנְחִיל֣וֹ אֶת־בָּנָ֔יו אֵ֥ת אֲשֶׁר־יִהְיֶ֖ה ל֑וֹ לֹ֣א יוּכַ֗ל לְבַכֵּר֙ אֶת־בֶּן־הָ֣אֲהוּבָ֔ה עַל־פְּנֵ֥י בֶן־הַשְּׂנוּאָ֖ה הַבְּכֹֽר׃
records.gloss: and it will be, on [the] day he causes to inherit his sons what is to him, not he is able to make firstborn [the] son of the loved [one] over [the] face of [the] son of the hated, the firstborn.
pieces: then when he divides his property among his sons as their inheritance, he must not give the rights of the firstborn to the son of the wife he loves in place of the son of the unloved wife, who is the true firstborn.

L.16: then it shall be, on the day he gives his sons as an inheritance what he has, he may not make the son of the loved [wife] firstborn in place of the son of the hated [wife], the firstborn.

R.16: When that man divides what he owns among his sons, he must not treat the son of the wife he loves as his firstborn son. The real firstborn is the son of the other wife.

decisions.choice: the day he gives his sons their inheritance: when he settles how his property will pass to them
decisions.reason: The verb means to make someone an heir. A father could divide his goods while he was alive or declare it before he died (Genesis 25:5-6; 48:21-22). This law limits what he may decide on that day.

decisions.choice: he may not: he has no right to
decisions.reason: "He is not able" here is a legal limit: the father is not allowed to do it, however he feels about the two wives.

decisions.choice: favoring the loved wife's son: the trouble in Jacob's family
decisions.reason: Jacob loved Rachel more than Leah and favored Rachel's son Joseph (Genesis 37:3). The right of the firstborn passed from Reuben, Leah's son, to the sons of Joseph, but only because of Reuben's sin (Genesis 49:3-4; 1 Chronicles 5:1-2). This law forbids a father to make such a change merely out of love for one wife.

decisions.choice: the rights of the firstborn / treat ... as his firstborn
decisions.reason: The Hebrew verb means "to make firstborn". Balanced says what that means in practice, giving the firstborn's rights; Readable says "treat as his firstborn".

decisions.choice: [wife]
decisions.reason: Literal adds "[wife]" after "the loved" and "the hated", which in Hebrew are feminine words that stand alone.

records.source: כִּי֩ אֶת־הַבְּכֹ֨ר בֶּן־הַשְּׂנוּאָ֜ה יַכִּ֗יר לָ֤תֶת לוֹ֙ פִּ֣י שְׁנַ֔יִם בְּכֹ֥ל אֲשֶׁר־יִמָּצֵ֖א ל֑וֹ כִּי־הוּא֙ רֵאשִׁ֣ית אֹנ֔וֹ ל֖וֹ מִשְׁפַּ֥ט הַבְּכֹרָֽה׃ס
records.gloss: For the firstborn, [the] son of the hated, he shall acknowledge, by giving to him a mouth of two in all that is found to him, for he [is] [the] beginning of his strength; to him [is] [the] right of the firstborn.
pieces: He must acknowledge the son of the unloved wife as the firstborn by giving him a double share of all he has. That son is the first sign of his father's strength, and the right of the firstborn belongs to him.

L.17: But the firstborn, the son of the hated [wife], he shall acknowledge by giving him a double portion of all that is found to be his, for he [is] the beginning of his strength; the right of the firstborn [is] his.

R.17: He must accept that son as his firstborn and give him twice as much as he gives each of his other sons. That son was the first sign of his father's strength. The rights of the firstborn son belong to him.

decisions.choice: acknowledge: recognize openly, as a legal act
decisions.reason: The verb means to recognize someone for who he is. Here the father must declare that this son is his firstborn and give him what belongs to the firstborn.

decisions.choice: a mouth of two: a double portion
decisions.reason: The Hebrew says "a mouth of two", meaning a share of two parts. It most likely means that the firstborn receives twice what each of his brothers receives. In Zechariah 13:8 the same phrase means two-thirds, so here it could mean two-thirds of the estate; that would only fit a family of two sons. Elisha's request for "a double portion" of Elijah's spirit uses the same words (2 Kings 2:9).

decisions.choice: the beginning of his strength: the first son of his father's manhood
decisions.reason: "Strength" here is a man's vigor and power to father children. Jacob uses the same words of his firstborn Reuben (Genesis 49:3; compare Psalm 105:36). The firstborn was seen as the first fruit of that strength.

decisions.choice: the right of the firstborn: the legal claim that belongs to the firstborn
decisions.reason: The first word means a rule or a rightful claim. The phrase sums up the law: the claim belongs to the firstborn son by birth and cannot be given away by the father's choice.

decisions.choice: a double share / twice as much as he gives each of his other sons
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable give the likely sense of "a mouth of two" (m2); Readable spells out what a double share is. Literal says "a double portion".

records.source: כִּֽי־יִהְיֶ֣ה לְאִ֗ישׁ בֵּ֚ן סוֹרֵ֣ר וּמוֹרֶ֔ה אֵינֶ֣נּוּ שֹׁמֵ֔עַ בְּק֥וֹל אָבִ֖יו וּבְק֣וֹל אִמּ֑וֹ וְיסְּר֣וּאֹת֔וֹ וְלֹ֥א יִשְׁמַ֖ע אֲלֵיהֶֽם׃
records.gloss: If is to a man a son stubborn and rebellious, not he [is] listening to [the] voice of his father and to [the] voice of his mother, and they discipline him and not he listens to them,
pieces: Suppose a man has a son who is stubborn and rebellious, who will not obey his father or his mother and will not listen to them even when they discipline him,

L.18: If a man has a stubborn and rebellious son, who does not listen to the voice of his father or to the voice of his mother, and they discipline him but he does not listen to them,

R.18: A man may have a son who is stubborn and rebels against his parents. He does not obey his father or his mother. They correct him, but he still will not listen to them.

decisions.choice: stubborn and rebellious: set in defiance
decisions.reason: The first word means turning aside, refusing to be led; the second means rebelling against authority. The same pair describes Israel's defiance of God (Psalm 78:8; Jeremiah 5:23). It names a settled way of life, not a single act; verse 20 shows the son is old enough to live as a glutton and a drunkard.

decisions.choice: listen to the voice: obey
decisions.reason: To "listen to the voice" of someone is to do what they say (13:5, 19).

decisions.choice: discipline: correct and train, with punishment if needed
decisions.reason: The verb covers teaching, warning and punishment together, the way a father trains a son (8:5; Proverbs 19:18). The parents have already tried to correct him.

decisions.choice: his father and his mother: both parents together
decisions.reason: The law names both parents here and in verses 19-20. It upholds the command to honor father and mother (5:16), and it does not let one angry parent bring the case alone.

records.heading: A stubborn and rebellious son

records.source: וְתָ֥פְשׂוּ ב֖וֹ אָבִ֣יו וְאִמּ֑וֹ וְהוֹצִ֧יאוּ אֹת֛וֹ אֶל־זִקְנֵ֥י עִיר֖וֹ וְאֶל־שַׁ֥עַר מְקֹמֽוֹ׃
records.gloss: and shall seize him his father and his mother and bring out him to [the] elders of his city and to [the] gate of his place,
pieces: his father and mother are to seize him and bring him out to the elders of his town, to the gate of the place where he lives,

L.19: then his father and his mother shall take hold of him and bring him out to the elders of his city and to the gate of his place,

R.19: Then his father and mother must take him to the elders of their town at the town gate.

decisions.choice: the elders at the gate: the town's court
decisions.reason: The open space inside a town gate was where the elders met to hear cases and witness agreements (22:15; 25:7; Ruth 4:1-2).

decisions.choice: the parents bring him to the elders: the case is judged, not settled at home
decisions.reason: The parents do not punish the son themselves. They must bring him before the town's leaders, who hear the charge. The father's authority is limited by the court of the community.

decisions.choice: the gate of the place where he lives / the town gate
decisions.reason: "The gate of his place" means the gate of his own town. Balanced says it in plain words; Readable joins it to the elders as the place where they meet.

records.source: וְאָמְר֞וּ אֶל־זִקְנֵ֣י עִיר֗וֹ בְּנֵ֤נוּ זֶה֙ סוֹרֵ֣ר וּמֹרֶ֔ה אֵינֶ֥נּוּ שֹׁמֵ֖עַ בְּקֹלֵ֑נוּ זוֹלֵ֖ל וְסֹבֵֽא׃
records.gloss: And they shall say to [the] elders of his city, son our this [is] stubborn and rebellious, not he [is] listening to our voice, [he is] a glutton and a drunkard.
pieces: They are to say to the elders of his town, 'This son of ours is stubborn and rebellious. He will not obey us. He is a glutton and a drunkard.'

L.20: And they shall say to the elders of his city, 'This son of ours [is] stubborn and rebellious; he does not listen to our voice; [he is] a glutton and a drunkard.'

R.20: They must tell the elders, 'Our son is stubborn and rebels against us. He will not obey us. He eats far too much and gets drunk.'

decisions.choice: a glutton and a drunkard: a reckless, wasteful life
decisions.reason: The first word means one who eats greedily and wastes, the second one who drinks heavily. Proverbs links the two with ruin and poverty (Proverbs 23:20-21). In a family that lived from its land and herds, such a son wastes what the household needs and shows his contempt for his parents in the open.

decisions.choice: the parents' words: a formal charge
decisions.reason: The parents repeat the charge of verse 18 before the elders, adding what everyone can see of his way of life. The elders hear the case and the men of the town carry out the sentence (verse 21).

decisions.choice: He will not obey us.
decisions.reason: "He does not listen to our voice" means he does not do what they say, so Balanced and Readable say "obey". Readable also says what "glutton and drunkard" means.

records.source: וּ֠רְגָמֻהוּ כָּל־אַנְשֵׁ֨י עִיר֤וֹ בָֽאֲבָנִים֙ וָמֵ֔ת וּבִֽעַרְתָּ֥ הָרָ֖ע מִקִּרְבֶּ֑ךָ וְכָל־יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל יִשְׁמְע֥וּ וְיִרָֽאוּ׃ס
records.gloss: And shall stone him all [the] men of his city with stones, and he shall die, and you shall purge the evil from your midst, and all Israel shall hear and fear.
pieces: All the men of his town are then to stone him to death. You must purge the evil from among you; all Israel will hear of it and be afraid.

L.21: And all the men of his city shall stone him with stones, and he shall die; so you shall purge the evil from your midst, and all Israel shall hear and fear.

R.21: Then all the men of his town must throw stones at him until he dies. You must get rid of this evil among you. All the people of Israel will hear about it and be afraid to do the same.

decisions.choice: stoned by all the men of the town
decisions.reason: Stoning was carried out by the community together, so that the whole people took part in the judgment (13:10-11; 17:5-7). Scripture records no case in which this law was carried out.

decisions.choice: purge the evil from your midst: remove the wrong and the wrongdoer from the community
decisions.reason: The same phrase closes several laws in Deuteronomy (13:6; 17:7; 19:19). "The evil" means both the deed and the one who does it.

decisions.choice: all Israel shall hear and fear: the sentence is a warning to everyone
decisions.reason: The punishment is meant to be known and to keep others from the same wrong, as in 13:12; 17:13 and 19:20. "Fear" here is being afraid of doing such a thing.

decisions.choice: stone him to death / throw stones at him until he dies
decisions.reason: "Stone him with stones, and he shall die" means to put him to death by stoning. Balanced says it in one phrase, and Readable describes what happens.

decisions.choice: be afraid to do the same
decisions.reason: Readable adds "to do the same" to show what the people will be afraid of (m3).

records.source: וְכִֽי־יִהְיֶ֣ה בְאִ֗ישׁ חֵ֛טְא מִשְׁפַּט־מָ֖וֶת וְהוּמָ֑ת וְתָלִ֥יתָ אֹת֖וֹ עַל־עֵֽץ׃
records.gloss: And if is in a man a sin of a sentence of death, and he is put to death, and you hang him on a tree,
pieces: If someone has committed a crime that carries the death penalty and has been put to death, and you hang the body on a tree,

L.22: And if there is in a man a sin [deserving] a sentence of death, and he is put to death, and you hang him on a tree,

R.22: Someone may be guilty of a crime that is punished by death. After that person is put to death, the body may be hung on a tree.

decisions.choice: put to death, then hung: the body is displayed after the execution
decisions.reason: The order of the verbs matters: the man is put to death first, and then his body is hung up. This is not a way of executing someone but of showing the body in public as a warning, as Joshua did with the kings he defeated (Joshua 10:26-27; compare 2 Samuel 4:12).

decisions.choice: a tree: a tree or a wooden post
decisions.reason: The word means a tree and also wood, so it can name a tree or a post or stake made of wood.

decisions.choice: a man: anyone
decisions.reason: The word is "man", but it is used here of anyone guilty of a crime that carries the death penalty.

decisions.choice: a sin of a sentence of death: a crime that deserves death
decisions.reason: The phrase joins "sin" with "judgment of death": a wrong for which the court's sentence is death (compare 19:6).

decisions.choice: someone; the body
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say "someone" for "a man" (m3) and "the body" for "him" in the last clause, to make clear that the person is already dead when he is hung up.

records.source: לֹא־תָלִ֨ין נִבְלָת֜וֹ עַל־הָעֵ֗ץ כִּֽי־קָב֤וֹר תִּקְבְּרֶ֨נּוּ֙ בַּיּ֣וֹם הַה֔וּא כִּֽי־קִלְלַ֥ת אֱלֹהִ֖ים תָּל֑וּי וְלֹ֤א תְטַמֵּא֙ אֶת־אַדְמָ֣תְךָ֔ אֲשֶׁר֙ יְהוָ֣ה אֱלֹהֶ֔יךָ נֹתֵ֥ן לְךָ֖ נַחֲלָֽה׃ס
records.gloss: Not shall remain overnight his corpse on the tree, but surely you shall bury him on the day the that, for a curse of God [is] a hanged [one]; and not you shall defile your land which Yahweh your God [is] giving to you [as] an inheritance.
pieces: you must not leave the body on the tree through the night. Be sure to bury it that same day, for anyone hung on a tree is under God's curse. You must not make unclean the land that {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} your God is giving you as an inheritance.

L.23: his body shall not remain all night on the tree, but you shall surely bury him on that same day, for a hanged [one] [is] a curse of God; and you shall not make your land unclean, which {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} your God is giving you [as] an inheritance.

R.23: Do not leave the body on the tree all night. You must bury it that same day, because anyone hung on a tree is under God's curse. Do not make the land unclean. {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} your God is giving it to you as your own.

decisions.choice: bury him the same day
decisions.reason: The body may not hang through the night. Joshua followed this law with the king of Ai and the five kings (Joshua 8:29; 10:27), and the Gospel of John records that the bodies of Jesus and the men crucified with him were taken down before evening (John 19:31).

decisions.choice: a curse of God: under God's curse
decisions.reason: The phrase can be read two ways. It most likely means that a man hung up after execution is one cursed by God: his crime and his punishment show him to be under God's judgment, and his body must not be left to bring that curse on the land. Later Jewish tradition read it instead as "an insult to God": leaving a human body hanging dishonors God. The ancient Greek translation has "cursed by God".

decisions.choice: quoted in Galatians 3:13 of the death of Christ
decisions.reason: Paul quotes this verse as "cursed is everyone who is hung on a tree" and applies it to Jesus' death on the cross: Christ redeemed those under the law's curse by becoming a curse for them. His wording is close to the ancient Greek translation of this verse. Peter and the apostles also speak of Jesus' death as "hanging him on a tree" (Acts 5:30; 10:39).

decisions.choice: do not defile your land: the land the LORD gives must be kept clean
decisions.reason: A dead body made unclean whatever it touched (Numbers 19:11-16). A body left exposed would make the land itself unclean, and the land belonged to the LORD, who gave it to Israel as a lasting possession (Numbers 35:33-34).

decisions.choice: anyone hung on a tree is under God's curse
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable give the likely sense (m2) and add "on a tree" from verse 22 so that "hung" is clear. Literal keeps the bare phrase "a curse of God", which leaves both readings open.

decisions.choice: the body ... it
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say "the body" and "it" for "his corpse" and "him", since the law applies to anyone executed (verse 22). Readable says "as your own" for "as an inheritance".
